replacement.headline: Hurricane Rafael shuts the nation's top crude export port and delays an Army brigade's move
replacement.dek: The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, halting crude exports, after Navy air stations flew aircraft inland and before an Army brigade could move its equipment through the port. Forecasters put the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch Saturday.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael on Saturday closed the busiest crude oil export gateway in the United States, as the Coast Guard shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and 14 vessels waited at an offshore anchorage in the Gulf.
The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of US crude exports, according to energy analysts, and its exports hit a monthly high in August. Loadings halted with the closure.

"This is the single most important crude export channel in the country right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "When it closes, the whole Atlantic basin trade notices."

The storm is also disrupting military operations on the Texas coast. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars, officials said.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, which is designated as a strategic seaport for military deployments, was postponed. The brigade had been scheduled to ship out for an overseas rotation.
Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said the brigade's soldiers would be ready to deploy as soon as the port is. He declined to give a new timeline.

Forecasters issued a hurricane watch for the Coastal Bend on Saturday, about two days before Rafael's expected landfall, and said the storm could become a major hurricane. Rafael became a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier in the week, and forecasters have warned it could strengthen rapidly.

Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval, the Coast Guard said, declining to identify them. "Vessels remaining in port do so with Coast Guard approval," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
Relief shipments have been booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on a cargo ship that cannot reach the port until the channel reopens.
Officials have not said when the channel will reopen. That will depend on the storm's track and on inspections afterward.

replacement.headline: Three kids, four bags and a bus that has not come yet
replacement.dek: Rosa Elizondo registered for an evacuation ride on Thursday. On Sunday, with surge zones under a mandatory evacuation and a hurricane warning up, she and her children waited for the county bus.
body: The bags are lined up by the front door, smallest to biggest. One for each of the three children, one for Rosa Elizondo. The smallest has a stuffed dog zipped halfway into the outside pocket so it can see.

A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Elizondo's rented home near the bay is in one. Forecasters upgraded Saturday's hurricane watch to a hurricane warning Sunday afternoon, about 36 hours before Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm. Shelters have opened inland. County buses are picking up residents without cars. Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who does not own a car, registered for a ride through 2-1-1 on Thursday, the day Rafael's forecast cone moved over Corpus Christi.
On Sunday, she waited.

"I did everything right. I called. I packed. Now I'm sitting on my suitcase like it's the airport," she said, then turned to the window, where her youngest had her face pressed to the glass. "Mija, sit down. The bus doesn't come faster if you look for it."

Up and down her block, the cars that were parked there on Friday were mostly gone by Sunday afternoon. Neighbors with cars had left on their own schedules, some on Saturday, some at first light. The street was quiet in a way Elizondo said she did not like.

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, a problem advocates raised all summer as they pushed for more evacuation rides. Sunday was the day that problem became a line of families watching a street.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said county buses were working through ride requests. "If you're registered and waiting, stay put and keep your phone on," he said. "We have your address."

In the afternoon, Elizondo's phone rang. It was Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall nearby and keeps a list of neighbors without cars. Whitfield wanted to know whether the family was ready and whether anyone had called. Elizondo said yes to the first and not yet to the second.
She spent part of the afternoon on the phone with her clients' families, making sure the people she cares for during the week had their own rides. "Them first," she said. "Then us."
By late afternoon, the family was still waiting. The children had eaten the sandwiches meant for the road. Elizondo made more and kept the bags by the door.
"I'm not scared yet," she said. "Ask me when the wind starts."
